video_title: Uranium’s Supply Crunch Is Getting Worse — And Prices Could Go Much Higher
gist: Uranium Insider's Justin Hune argues the Google–Constellation 890 MW deal is uprate-based and adds little uranium demand, but the secular bull case rests on life extensions, ~80 reactors under construction, Eastern energy-sovereignty buying and exhausted inventories; he targets $150-200+/lb and favors physical vehicles (SPUT, Yellow Cake) at NAV discounts plus operators and select SMR winners like GE Vernova.

themes.theme: Hyperscaler nuclear deals: narrative vs uranium demand

insights.claim: The Google–Constellation deal adds ~890 MW to the PJM grid entirely via uprates across 11 existing reactors (>$4B investment in steam generators, turbines), which does not materially increase uranium demand.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Headline-driven rallies on uprate deals overstate direct uranium demand; fade the uranium-specific read-through, keep the operator read-through.
insights.quote: these upgrades don't actually equal significantly more uranium demand

insights.claim: The ~12% pop in Constellation and the sector on the Google deal was amplified by short covering after months of extremely oversold conditions and washed-out sentiment, more than by deal fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Sentiment/positioning, not fundamentals, drives day-to-day moves; watch for follow-through rather than chasing headline days.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers are currently securing the 'low-hanging fruit': long-dated PPAs with incumbent operators whose reactors can be life-extended, with upfront money possibly funding licence extensions.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Incumbent nuclear operators are the cleanest beneficiaries of AI power demand; they will also be price-insensitive fuel buyers.

insights.claim: All US reactors are expected to reach 60-year licences, roughly 25-30% of the fleet has applied for 80-year extensions, operators plan for 80 years and some possibly 100, against an average fleet age of ~46 years.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Life extensions structurally lengthen uranium demand tails that models once assumed would close.

insights.claim: Over the past five years his models have had to add 20-year extensions to almost every reactor previously expected to close between 2025 and 2035.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Demand upside has come from fewer closures rather than new builds — a less visible but more certain driver.
insights.quote: we've had to go back over that period of time and adjust those models to add 20-year extensions to almost everything

insights.claim: Hyperscalers are also engaging with new nuclear: Amazon is heavily invested in X-energy, Meta is partially funding two TerraPower Natrium reactors, and Google has a looser deal with Kairos.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Track which SMR developers have hyperscaler capital as an early winner-selection filter.

insights.claim: NexGen Energy has said hyperscalers have contacted it about potential future uranium offtake from its Rook I project in Saskatchewan, and he expects a hyperscaler-uranium supply headline within 18-24 months.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: A direct hyperscaler uranium offtake would be a major re-rating catalyst for developers like NexGen.
insights.quote: I do think that that headline is coming probably in the next 18 to 24 months

insights.claim: Nuclear is correlated with but not reliant on the AI build-out; institutional 'AI picks-and-shovels' factor baskets lumped uranium miners and SMRs in, so when the AI story softened (Anthropic CEO calling for a handbrake) money left a small sector and retail capitulated.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Uranium equities carry AI-factor beta unrelated to fundamentals — creating mispricings when AI sentiment dips.
insights.quote: it's not reliant whatsoever. But it is correlated

insights.claim: Uranium demand can be modelled with high confidence 5-7 years out from operating reactors, life extensions and construction pipelines, against only ~50-60 supply projects globally, and his model cannot identify any project that eventually balances the market.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Rare commodity where the supply gap is mappable; the absence of a balancing project supports a sustained bull case.
insights.quote: We we actually have no idea when or how that's going to come

insights.claim: He targets uranium at minimum $150-$200/lb this cycle and likely higher, because the top will be set by what buyers pay for the last marginal pound rather than incentive prices.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Implies ~50-100%+ upside from ~$80-100 levels; incentive-price-based models may understate the peak.
insights.quote: We believe it's going to go minimally to $150 to $200 a pound during this cycle and probably higher

insights.claim: Mine supply rose ~40% from ~120M lb to over 170M lb since 2021, mostly brownfield restarts, yet price tripled — showing the market now relies on primary production as secondary/commercial inventories have shrunk dramatically since the 2010s.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Supply response hasn't capped price; greenfield projects are needed and brownfield restarts are largely used up.

insights.claim: Global nuclear capacity of roughly 400 GW is set to reach ~500 GW in about five years, with almost 80 reactors under construction — the most simultaneously in nearly three decades — and nuclear growth rising from 1-2% to 4-5% annually.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: A 25% capacity jump in five years against long-lead mine supply underpins the deficit thesis.

insights.claim: UxC, the primary price reporter, stated publicly that uranium (not conversion or enrichment) is the biggest bottleneck in the fuel cycle for coming years and will be the most price-impacted.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Focus is rotating from enrichment/conversion to U3O8 — the laggard in the fuel chain.
insights.quote: the biggest bottleneck that we see in the coming years is uranium

insights.claim: SMR, nuclear shipping and space/lunar reactor demand are essentially absent from his models; all of it is right-tail upside, not required for the thesis.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Base case doesn't depend on speculative demand, lowering thesis risk.
insights.quote: We have minimal SMR demand in our models. So it's all right tail if that snowballs.

themes.theme: Spot vs term market mechanics and trading signals

insights.claim: Long-term contract price is ~$96.50/lb (UxC/TradeTech blend); most term contracts are market-referenced at delivery with floors of $70-80 and ceilings of ~$150 for delivery 2-6 years out, i.e. a seller's market.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Term-contract ceilings at $150 signal utilities accept much higher prices; term is the better signal than spot.

insights.claim: Spot is a thin surplus-disposal market (~4-5M lb/month, e.g. Uzbek offtake dumped by traders); recently more sellers than buyers yet price hasn't fallen and traders are positioned for higher prices.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Price holding against net selling suggests a firm floor — supportive of buying the dip.

insights.claim: The carry trade links spot and term; when spot disconnects far below a flat term price (e.g. spot ~$64 vs term ~$80 last March-April) it is a buying signal, and equities subsequently doubled or tripled.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Spot-term discount = buy equities; spot spiking in backwardation over flat term = sell into euphoria.

insights.claim: A backwardated market where spot runs far above a flat term price during risk-on euphoria is unsustainable and a signal to sell.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Use spot-term spread as a contrarian timing tool.

insights.claim: January's rally was driven by the Sprott Physical Uranium Trust raising over half a billion dollars and buying 6M+ lb in under two months, pushing spot from ~$80 to over $100 before a February 'rug pull' that soured sentiment.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: SPUT flows can whipsaw spot; their raise-driven spikes tend to retrace.

insights.claim: The sector typically bottoms seasonally in August; this year it rallied 15-25% over 3-4 weeks then pulled back deeper than expected, producing public capitulation — and buying into such terrible sentiment has been a reliable strategy.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Seasonality plus capitulation sentiment offers repeatable entry points.
insights.quote: buying into terrible sentiment following, you know, even just a move like today. It's >> it's it's been a reliable strategy

insights.claim: Utility fuel buyers are not investors: they buy what they need when they need it, rarely hedge, and avoid price bets for career-risk reasons, which is why they didn't stockpile cheap uranium in the 2010s.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Utility demand is price-inelastic and pro-cyclical — it arrives in bulk when supply is already tight.

insights.claim: Since 2022 Western utilities shifted away from Russian enrichment, causing conversion and enrichment prices to roughly triple to near all-time highs; securing those services then pulls uranium demand, since the fuel cycle takes 18 months to 2.5+ years.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Enrichment/conversion tightness is a leading indicator for U3O8 buying.

themes.theme: Energy sovereignty: China, Russia, India buildouts

insights.claim: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to the war in Iran this year highlighted energy as sovereign security, accelerating life extensions and inventory building, especially in the East.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Geopolitics adds a non-AI, state-backed demand driver.

insights.claim: China has ~40 reactors under construction, roughly half the global total, while also building massive solar and coal capacity.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: China is the largest single incremental uranium demand source.

insights.claim: Russia, building ~23 reactors abroad and the largest enricher, second-largest converter and third-largest uranium producer, announced in August it is buying uranium from its JV partner in direct competition with utilities.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Russia turning buyer removes supply from Western markets and tightens the balance.

insights.claim: India's national nuclear operator signed contracts totaling nearly 50M lb with Kazatomprom and Cameco between Q4 and Q1 — far more than its existing fleet needs — and amended liability laws to welcome foreign builders.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: India shifting from talk to action is new term demand; validates Cameco/Kazatomprom contract books.

insights.claim: A US–South Korea deal would see significant Korean investment in building six Westinghouse AP1000s and two APR1400s, though not yet finalised.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Potential large-reactor new-build catalyst for Westinghouse/Cameco.

insights.claim: Taiwan is restarting a reactor, Belgium likely will, and France has generally approved its two reactor designs (~90% of its fleet) to run to 60 years.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Policy reversals globally extend demand duration.

insights.claim: NIMBY is not a top-10 obstacle for US nuclear, since dozens of existing sites are already permitted for more capacity and local communities support plants; Diablo Canyon (10% of California's grid) should get its 60-year extension signed by the next governor.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Brownfield site expansion de-risks US new-build; Diablo Canyon extension is a near-term event.
insights.quote: It's 10% of the grid in the state. They have to extend it. And I think they will.

insights.claim: The physical commodity offers the best risk/reward now via Sprott Physical Uranium Trust (~8-9% discount to NAV, ranging to 15-16% in risk-off) and Yellow Cake PLC, which has historically traded at a wider discount and has a $100M/yr purchase deal with Kazatomprom ending next year.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Buying physical vehicles at NAV discounts gives leveraged-to-floor exposure; discount narrowing to NAV triggers new buying.
insights.quote: the investment in the physical commodity in my opinion is probably the best riskreward proposition, the least risk

insights.claim: Barring a nuclear accident or market meltdown, spot uranium has a pretty firm floor and shouldn't move much lower from current levels.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Asymmetric entry: limited downside versus $150-200 target.

insights.claim: Of 70-90 companies pushing ~150 SMR designs, about half a dozen will be primary winners and should become clear within five years; selection should weigh customer deals, construction progress and regulatory approvals.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Use a small diversified SMR basket rather than single bets; most will fail.

insights.claim: GE Vernova's BWRX-300 is an obvious SMR winner: first unit under construction at Darlington, Ontario, likely Clinch River for TVA with early NRC approvals, and daily inbound calls and site visits.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: GE Vernova is a diversified, hold-for-decades way to own SMR upside.
insights.quote: the line is going to be around the block once we have our first of a kind built

insights.claim: TerraPower's Natrium (Wyoming) and X-energy's Xe-100 (Amazon-backed, ~$500-700M; 10-12 reactor plant in Washington; Dow site in Texas expecting early construction permit in Q1 next year) are the two US demonstration leaders.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: X-energy Q1 permit is a dated catalyst; watch for IPO/private funding events.

insights.claim: For liquidity-needing institutions, operators like Vistra, Constellation, Duke or Dominion offer better risk/reward than early-stage SMR pure plays, some of which became Reddit meme stocks in late 2024-early 2025.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Prefer established operators over speculative SMRs for core exposure.

insights.claim: Solid nuclear names such as BWXT and nuclear utility stocks have sold off 20-30%+ from highs and some pay dividends; small nuclear stocks need to double to quadruple to regain year-ago levels, so a mixed basket is a no-brainer here.
insights.speaker: Justin Hune
insights.so_what: Washed-out large caps offer quality exposure at a discount.
